item.description:
作者：Nikunj Kothari 账号：@nikunj 简介：partner @fpvventures - investing in seed/A. previous: early hire @meter, @opendoor, @atlassian & others. love @shimoleejhaveri + 👦👧
I scraped 803 companies sub-processors to investigate what AI native companies are using for their infrastructure..
Some interesting findings from the last time I did this in March:
> 44% of companies list two+ model providers (up from 33%). Small n, but Anthropic grew twice as fast as OpenAI.
> 86 pairs where each company names the other as a subprocessor (@AnthropicAI + @Cloudflare, @vercel + @spacexai)
> 33% of companies list an inference provider (up from 22%). @modal continues to crush.
> Chinese models are primarily coming through video (think Bytedance) rather than text (at least on the subprocessor lists)
> @typesafeai is the breakout hit, going from 0 to many companies in a short period.
Caveat: subprocessor lists tend to be a lagging indicator, but a sure shot way of knowing if the company is using something.
You can find all the updated data, design and insights at deploygraph dot com. Feedback welcome!

item.title: There are basically two kinds of companies to build right now. 1. Diffusion of AI This is the "vertical SaaS" of today. There are a bunch of different models for it (FDE company, rollup, horizontal product) but ultimately it all boils down to the same thing: get AI diffused very close to where the ...
item.description:
作者：Aditya Agarwal 账号：@adityaag 简介：General Partner @SPC, Co-Founder @Bevel_Health | Ex: Early Eng @facebook, CTO @Dropbox, Board @Flipkart | Optimist, Builder, Dad
There are basically two kinds of companies to build right now.
1. Diffusion of AI This is the "vertical SaaS" of today. There are a bunch of different models for it (FDE company, rollup, horizontal product) but ultimately it all boils down to the same thing: get AI diffused very close to where the work is being done.
Profound, Cognition, Harvey etc. A lot of great companies will get built here.
2. Frontier of AI This is where the really interesting action is. Use AI to accelerate scientific progress, then build products from that progress.
It is a harder category to see. But we are seeing a lot more of it at @spc:
- Externa is adding hundreds of new chemical building blocks to proteins, so you can engineer a drug to match the disease instead of settling for what nature gave you.
- Epana Bio is using genomics and AI to design autoimmune therapies that go after the cellular origin of the disease.
- VenomicsAI is doing AI-accelerated drug discovery from venoms.
- Equivariant is doing multi-physics modeling for the semiconductor industry.
(There are always picks-and-shovels for AI as well. Lots of amazing companies in that category.)
Category 2 is not well understood or much talked about externally. It should be because I think that is where the vast majority of model driven returns will come from.

Last week, between meetings, I analyzed our customer survey, made a game for our team, spotted an opportunity to sell @Every to te...
item.description:
作者：Dan Shipper 账号：@danshipper 简介：ceo @every | the only subscription you need to stay at the edge of AI
I look at what I do with Fable 5.2 in the cracks of my week and think: this would've taken five people and $200,000.
Then I look at what my team does with the same AI.
Last week, between meetings, I analyzed our customer survey, made a game for our team, spotted an opportunity to sell @Every to teams, built a CRM, and started reaching out.
Look at that and you might ask: Why would I need a team at all?
The chart seems to agree. On OpenAI's GDPval benchmark, AI went from beating human experts 12.4% of the time in 2024 to around 83% in 2026. That's the aggregate view of the future of work: gather a lot of data and extrapolate a trend line.
But the aggregate misses something. To see it, you have to get intimate: zoom in on one real situation, with all its messiness, and extrapolate from there.
We gave everyone at Every access to the same customer survey and the same AI models.
• I found an opportunity to sell to teams. • @poojary_yash saw that first-time subscribers were churning because we send too much email. • @dabrundage noticed that many of our readers feel lonely: they're excited about AI, but people around them think they're crazy. • @jackcheng turned the results into a Claymation game show.
Could you ask Claude to produce what each of them found? Maybe. But generating possibilities is cheap. Knowing which ones matter is hard.
@hammer_mt ran an experiment to predict what I'd say in Slack. When Claude got 400 attempts, it produced an answer like mine 93% of the time. But when it had to rank its own answers, mine landed in its top 10% only around 60% of the time.
Each person on a team is responsible for a different part of the world. That responsibility narrows where they look, and their perspective helps them decide what matters enough to act on. A team explores more possibilities than a single default prompt, and it can take responsibility for what it finds.
The obvious objection: models will get better at ranking. I think they will. But people aren't frozen while that happens. Comparing 2026 Yash with 2027 Claude misses that there will also be a 2027 Yash, with another year of experience, using 2027 Claude.
As models improve and spread, they raise the floor for everyone. The default answer becomes the baseline. The value is in using your perspective and responsibility to push past it.
That's why I think we need to change how we measure AI. Instead of only asking how well a model performs on problems everyone agrees are worth solving, ask: How good is it at doing my work, from my perspective?
The aggregate can show us the capability curve. The intimate helps us see what we might build, and who we might become, as we ride it.
I presented this at Thesis: 2027. The full talk is on the Every podcast:

item.title: A New Vision for Human Work After Automation
item.description:
播客：AI & I by Every
Hey, welcome back to the Every Podcast, where we talk about the future of work.
I'm Natalia Quintero, and at Every, our team of writers and builders use AI every day, so we can tell you how the frontier is shifting, what actually works, and what you need to know.
So last week at Every, we hosted our first ever conference, V.C.S.S.,
It was a full day of talks in Brooklyn featuring speakers from Anthropic, OpenAI, Notion, Lovable, Ode, and many more.
If you missed it, we'll have all of the talks available at every.to forward slash TV.
We built the whole day around one question.
What does great human work look like after automation?
Dan Shipper, Every's co-founder and CEO, closed the conference with his answer, which you'll hear later in this episode.
He took our quarterly customer survey results and built a custom CRM, then a video game, and then personally reached out to a pretty vast number of our customers.
In pre-AI terms, he did the work of about five people, a data scientist, a game developer, a marketer, an engineer, and a salesperson.
But instead, he did all of that work with a single clot subscription over the course of a single week.
And if you ask Claude what it sees in the same survey, you'll probably get a generic answer that anyone could get.
And that's actually Dan's point.
Great work is the perspective you bring to the model.
So for the podcast this week, Dan's closing talk from our conference thesis.
Enjoy.
Thesis, did everyone have a good time?
Woo!
Well, we gathered here to answer one question, which is what is the future of great human work after automation?
I hope you got some good answers today.
Did you get some good answers?
Yes?
Yes?
All right.
I wanna add my take.
Hopefully I can help bring it together a little bit.
So I really, I love this question.
And obviously, because we built the conference around it, it's really the question that we try to answer every day at every,
And what's really interesting about this question is you're really trying to predict the future.
And there's two, I think, real methods for predicting the future.
One is what I'll call the aggregate, where you gather lots and lots of data, and then you extrapolate a trend line.
And the other is called the intimate, where you zoom in on one real case or real situation, and then you extrapolate from there.
And in our culture, we tend to emphasize the aggregate.
The aggregate is objective, it's quantitative, and the intimate kind of feels a little bit anecdotal.
And the aggregate's also extremely powerful.
The reason we have AI is the aggregate, is for example, scaling loss.
We found that if you put more data and compute on one end of the system, you get more capability out.
And all of us here are here because we're riding that curve that you can see in the aggregate.
We also use the aggregate to answer this question that we have come here for.
What does work look like after automation?
A good example is GDP Val from OpenAI.
It's a benchmark which measures how good models are at doing economically valuable tasks.
And the way it works is they have a bunch of experts pick tasks from their job, real tasks, and they turn it into a prompt.
They give the prompts to a model, and they give a prompt to a human that's not using AI, and then blind experts pick which one is better, the human version or the AI version.
And the prompts are very, very detailed.
They look something like this.
And in 2024, with GPT-4-0, experts, or AI, won against a human expert 12.4% of the time.
In 2025 it was 47.6 and in 2026 it was about 83%.
This is with GPT 5.4, I'm sure it's higher now.
I'm sure this benchmark is saturated.
You look at that, an AI is beating a human 83% of the time according to blind human experts at expert work.
And I can also see this in my work, in the way that I work.
If we look at my week, last week.
We ran our quarterly customer survey.
And in the cracks of my calendar, in the middle of all of the things that I had going on, I analyzed the survey data in a way that once would have required a data scientist or a growth person to do it.
Like I asked a ton of different questions and got a ton of different reports and outputs.
I made a video game for the team to play.
So we played in our all hands game to compete to see who knew our customers best.
It was a live, real time video game.
I realized that there's actually a really interesting opportunity to sell every to teams from all of this work.
And then, as one does, I vibe coded my own CRM and started using that to reach out to people.
You may have gotten an email from me last week.
If so, apologies.
It's kind of stunning.
It's amazing.
But if you look at it and compare it to human work.
This is in 2020 terms like a data scientist, a game developer, a product marketer, an engineer, a BDR, and like 200, maybe 200K.
And I got all of this for free as part of my cloud subscription.
And you think about that, you really think about that, you look at a table like this and you are like, we are so fucked.
We are so fucked.
And, yeah.
To me, it does this thing that I've been calling it.
It creates an agency rupture because we identify ourselves with the things that we do, with the work that we do.
And if you see a model doing work like you do, it strikes at our sense of self.
And I also think that while the aggregate is a very useful lens, especially when it comes to new technology, it also misses things.
It can be misleading.
And you can only see what's missing if you get up close.
So let's do that.
So, again, we've got these two different ways of predicting the future of the aggregate.
Okay.
Let's go into the Intimate.
Let's see how things look in the Intimate where you zoom in on one real case, you really understand all the messiness of it and all the different interconnecting variables and then try to extrapolate from there.
So if you look back at this table,
and you think about my week last week, doing all of this, which would have taken five people in 2020, and I'm doing all of that work with a team of agents in the cracks of my week while I'm doing a totally other separate set of tasks.
I think that this is actually how a lot of people in this room are working already, and probably if you're not, you will be in the near future.
And it feels almost normal to work this way.
Like it's not even that remarkable that I analyzed my survey or built the vibe coder to see a master sent some cold emails with my agents.
But this was actually really not normal, even a few years ago.
So think about in 2022, like before ChetGPT came out, we only had GPT-3.
And there were a lot of people looking at this chart, this aggregate chart and saying, this is not gonna continue, it's just a stochastic parrot.
And a lot of other people were like, this is the end of all jobs already.
We're not gonna have any work to do in two years, it's all over, go to the bunker in New Zealand, that's it.
And for me and for every, we take this intimate perspective.
We try to be up close.
And so in 2022, I was using GPT-3
And I realized that it felt like if I extrapolated out from using that tool, it would feel like using a team of people in a couple of years just by using an AI.
So I wrote that rather than replacing individuals, recent advances in AI will empower them to make an impact on scale matching some of the biggest businesses, research labs, and creative organizations of today.
I really think that's true now.
You could see it if you put your hands in GPT-3 and used it and extrapolated it.
I want to try to do that again today here with all of us.
If we take this and how we're working today, what does that mean for the future of great human work and are we really fucked?
And what's really interesting is, again, if I look at this table in a vacuum, you might assume, like, why would I need a team?
I have a team, I've got the agents right here.
But there mu...
